title: Why attention changed everything
summary: A short, intuition-first look at why attention replaced recurrence for sequence modeling — and what it actually computes.
content:
Before transformers, sequence models leaned on recurrence. RNNs and LSTMs processed tokens one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward. That worked, but it made two things hard: **long-range dependencies** and **parallelism**.

## The core idea

Attention reframes the problem. Instead of compressing the past into a single state, each token looks at *every other token* and decides what to focus on. The mechanism is deceptively simple:

```python
import numpy as np

def attention(Q, K, V):
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return weights @ V
```

The scaled dot-product gives us a similarity between queries and keys; the softmax turns it into weights; the weights mix the values.

## Why it matters

- **Parallel by design.** Every position is computed at once, so training scales with modern hardware.
- **Direct connections.** Any token can attend to any other in a single step, so long-range structure is cheap.
- **Interpretable-ish.** Attention maps hint at what the model is using, even if they aren't a full explanation.

> The lesson I keep coming back to: the right inductive bias can matter more than raw capacity.

There's much more nuance — multi-head attention, positional encodings, and the quadratic cost that later work tries to tame. But the leap in intuition is this: *let the model decide what to look at.*

title: Notes on reproducible ML experiments
summary: Small habits that make experiments trustworthy: seeds, config, tracking, and honest evaluation.
content:
A model result you can't reproduce is a story, not a finding. Over time I've collected a few habits that keep experiments honest.

## Pin the randomness

Set seeds everywhere and log them. It won't guarantee bit-for-bit reproducibility on GPUs, but it removes the easy excuses.

```python
import random, numpy as np, torch

def set_seed(seed: int = 42):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
```

## Separate config from code

Keep hyperparameters in a config file, not scattered across the script. Every run should be describable by *(code version, config, data version)*.

## Track everything

- metrics over time, not just the final number
- the exact command and environment
- data splits, so the test set never leaks

## Evaluate honestly

Report variance across seeds, not a single lucky run. If a gain is within noise, say so. The goal isn't a bigger number — it's a claim you can defend.

title: Reading papers without drowning
summary: A practical three-pass method for getting signal from ML papers without burning a whole day on each one.
content:
Machine learning moves fast, and the paper firehose is real. Here's the workflow that keeps me afloat.

## Pass one — the map

Read the title, abstract, figures, and conclusion. Ask one question: *what problem does this solve, and does it matter to me right now?* Most papers can stop here.

## Pass two — the method

For papers that survive, read the method and results carefully. Reimplement the key equation or a toy version if you can. Understanding comes from rebuilding, not re-reading.

## Pass three — the critique

Only for the few that will shape your work. Question the assumptions, the baselines, and the evaluation. Would the result hold on your data?

---

The point isn't to read *more* papers. It's to spend your attention where it compounds.
